label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
For $n=2^r$, every randomized algorithm that, with probability at least
$2/3$ on every labelling, outputs $r$ elements forming a basis of a
group isomorphic to $\mathbb F_2^r$ requires $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ group additions
in the worst case. This holds even when all element labels and the
identity label are supplied for free, and all computation other than
group additions is free.
head: environment
name: Basis construction

label: thm:iso
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:iso}
The isomorphism type of a finite Abelian group of known order $n$
can be computed with probability at least $2/3$ using
$\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$ group additions and
$\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$ total time.
Consequently, two finite Abelian groups of known order can be tested
for isomorphism with probability at least $2/3$ within the same bounds,
where $n$ is their common order.
head: environment
name: Isomorphism type and decision

label: thm:structure
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:structure}
Let $G$ be a finite Abelian group of order
$n=\prod_{p\mid n}p^{a_p}$, where $p$ ranges over the prime divisors of $n$.
For each such $p$, the elements whose orders are powers of $p$, together
with $0$, form a subgroup $G_p$ of order $p^{a_p}$. Moreover,
 $G\cong\bigoplus_{p\mid n}G_p$.

For each $p$ there is a unique nonincreasing list of positive integers
$\lambda_{p,1},\ldots,\lambda_{p,t_p}$ such that
$G_p\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^{t_p}\mathbb Z_{p^{\lambda_{p,i}}}$.
The sum of the entries $\lambda_{p,i}$ in this list is $a_p$.
head: environment
name: Fundamental theorem of finite Abelian groups

label: ex:type
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:type}
The group $\mathbb Z_8\oplus\mathbb Z_4\oplus\mathbb Z_2\oplus\mathbb Z_2$ has order $2^7$ and type
$(3,2,1,1)$ at the prime $2$. Its four coordinate vectors form a basis.
If its $128$ elements are renamed by arbitrary labels, the type remains
$(3,2,1,1)$, but the labels of those coordinate vectors are hidden. Producing
the four integers and producing four suitable labels are different tasks.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Take $d=2$ and suppose the algorithm requests the addition of two
distinct, previously unregistered labels $a$ and $b$.
We assign $D(a)=X_1$ and $D(b)=X_2$. Their addition returns a new
label $c$, with $D(c)=X_1+X_2$. If the algorithm subsequently adds
the elements labelled $c$ and $a$, the simulation returns $b$,
because
    $(X_1+X_2)+X_1=X_2$.
This answer follows from the rules for formal addition.
head: environment

label: lem:coupling
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:coupling}
Suppose $M\leq n$. The symbolic simulation, together with its
independent random evaluations, can be coupled to an actual
execution on a uniformly random labelling of $H$ so that, whenever
$\mathsf{Bad}$ does not occur, the requested additions, returned labels,
and outputs are identical. Moreover, in this case,
\[
    \phi(\ell)=\mathsf{ev}(D(\ell))
\]
for every registered label $\ell$.
head: environment
name: Coupling

title: Proof
body_md:
We construct the random bijection $\phi$ gradually, assigning a
group element to a label only when needed. Initially,
$\phi(\iota)=0$. At every stage, all bijections extending the
assignments already made must remain equally likely.

For this proof, we may also choose $h_j$ when the formal symbol
$X_j$ is first introduced. This gives the same symbolic experiment
as choosing all the $h_j$ after the simulation: each $h_j$ is chosen
independently and uniformly from $H$, and the symbolic simulation
never uses these values to choose its answers.

We try to keep both executions identical and to maintain
$\phi(\ell)=\mathsf{ev}(D(\ell))$ for every registered label.
We declare a divergence if these conditions can no longer be
maintained.

\paragraph{A new operand or output label.}
Suppose the executions still agree, and $\phi$ has been assigned
on $b$ labels. Let $\ell$ be a new label chosen by the algorithm
as an operand or included in its output. In a uniformly random
bijection, $\phi(\ell)$ must be uniform among the $n-b$ elements
of $H$ that have not yet been assigned to labels.

The simulation assigns the next unused symbol $X_j$ to $\ell$.
Choose its value $h_j$ independently and uniformly from all of $H$.
If $h_j$ has not yet been assigned to a label, set
$\phi(\ell)=h_j$. Otherwise, declare divergence and choose
$\phi(\ell)$ uniformly among the unused elements of $H$.

This rule gives the correct distribution for $\phi(\ell)$.
Indeed, for any unused element $a\in H$, conditional on the
preceding history, the probability that $\phi(\ell)=a$ is
\[
    \frac1n+\frac bn\frac1{n-b}
    =\frac1{n-b}.
\]
The first term corresponds to choosing $h_j=a$. The second
corresponds to choosing an already assigned element and then
choosing $a$ as the replacement.

If divergence occurs, $h_j$ equals the value of an earlier
registered expression. That expression is different from the
new symbol $X_j$, so this gives a collision in the symbolic
simulation. This argument also applies to output labels that
were not used earlier.

\paragraph{An addition answer.}
Suppose the executions still agree and the algorithm requests
the addition of labels $x$ and $y$. Let
    $w=D(x)+D(y)$.
Because evaluation preserves addition, the actual sum has value
$\phi(x)+\phi(y)=\mathsf{ev}(w)$.
If $w$ already has a registered label, both executions return
that label.
Otherwise, the simulation chooses a uniformly random unregistered
label $z$ and assigns $D(z)=w$. This choice is made without using
$\mathsf{ev}(w)$.

If $\mathsf{ev}(w)$ has not yet been assigned to a label in the actual
execution, set $\phi(z)=\mathsf{ev}(w)$ and return $z$ there as well.
This preserves the correct distribution of the random bijection:
the label of a specified unused group element is uniform among
the unregistered labels.

If $\mathsf{ev}(w)$ is already assigned to a label, the actual execution
returns that existing label, whereas the simulation returns the
new label $z$. Declare divergence. The expression associated
with the existing label is different from $w$, but has the same
evaluation. Thus, a collision has occurred.

\paragraph{Completing the executions.}
After a divergence, continue the actual execution by extending
its partially assigned bijection uniformly as needed. Continue
the symbolic simulation using its original rules, choosing new
answer labels without consulting the values $h_j$.

Each execution therefore retains its required distribution.
Every first divergence produces a collision in the symbolic
simulation. Consequently, if $\mathsf{Bad}$ does not occur, the executions
and outputs agree, and
$\phi(\ell)=\mathsf{ev}(D(\ell))$ holds for every registered label.
Complete $\phi$ uniformly on any remaining labels.

Throughout this construction, the symbolic experiment retains
its original distribution; we never condition it on the absence
of collisions.
head: environment

label: lem:collision
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:collision}
If the symbolic simulation registers at most $M$ distinct formal
expressions, then
\[
    \mathop{\rm Pr}[\mathsf{Bad}]\leq\frac{\binom M2}{n}.
\]
head: environment
name: Unconditional collision bound

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix the complete record $T$ of the symbolic simulation.
Let $u$ and $v$ be two distinct registered expressions.
Since their coefficient lists differ, we can write
    $u-v=\sum_j c_jX_j$
with at least one coefficient equal to one. Choose an index $t$
such that $c_t=1$.
If we fix all the vectors $h_j$ except $h_t$, then
\[
    \mathsf{ev}(u-v)=h_t+\sum_{j\ne t}c_jh_j.
\]
The second term is fixed, and $h_t$ is uniform in $V$. Adding a
fixed vector to a uniform vector gives another uniform vector.
Consequently,
$\mathop{\rm Pr}[\mathsf{ev}(u)=\mathsf{ev}(v)\mid T]=1/n$. There are at most $\binom M2$ pairs of distinct registered
expressions. By the union bound,
\[
    \mathop{\rm Pr}[\mathsf{Bad}\mid T]\leq\frac{\binom M2}{n}.
\]
This holds for every possible $T$. Averaging over $T$ proves
the stated bound. We have not conditioned on the absence of
collisions.
head: environment

label: lem:ideal-output
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Simulated output probability

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $T$, and suppose the simulation introduced the symbols
$X_1,\ldots,X_t$. Write the output expressions as
\[
    u_i=\sum_{j=1}^t a_{ij}X_j,
    \qquad i=1,\ldots,r,
\]
and let $A=(a_{ij})$ be their $r\times t$ coefficient matrix
over $\mathbb F_2$. Since $T$ is fixed, $A$ is fixed independently of
the random vectors $h_1,\ldots,h_t$.
If the row rank of $A$ is less than $r$, some nonzero linear
combination of its rows is zero. The same combination of the
evaluated vectors $\mathsf{ev}(u_1),\ldots,\mathsf{ev}(u_r)$ is then zero.
These vectors are linearly dependent and cannot form a basis.

Suppose instead that $A$ has row rank $r$. Choose $r$ columns
forming an invertible $r\times r$ matrix. Fix the vectors $h_j$
corresponding to all the other columns.
For any prescribed output tuple $(y_1,\ldots,y_r)\in V^r$,
the equations
\[
    \sum_{j=1}^t a_{ij}h_j=y_i,
    \qquad i=1,\ldots,r,
\]
now have exactly one solution for the $r$ remaining vectors
$h_j$. Indeed, we can solve the invertible linear system
separately in each coordinate of $V$.
The $r$ remaining vectors are independent and uniform in $V$.
Thus, every output tuple in $V^r$ has probability $n^{-r}$.
The evaluated output vectors are therefore independent and
uniform in $V$, and their probability of forming a basis is
exactly $\rho_r$.

For every fixed $T$, the basis probability is consequently
either zero or $\rho_r$. Averaging over $T$ proves the lemma.
head: environment

label: thm:quantitative
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Quantitative success bound

title: Proof
body_md:
First fix the algorithm's random choices. Use the joint
construction from Lemma~\ref{lem:coupling}. 
By~\eqref{eq:count}, the simulation registers at most
$3q+r+1$ distinct expressions. Lemma~\ref{lem:ideal-output}
bounds the first probability by $\rho_r$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:collision} bounds the second by
$\binom{3q+r+1}{2}/n$. This proves~\eqref{eq:success}
for every fixed choice of the algorithm's random bits.
Averaging over those choices proves the randomized statement.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $r\geq2$, equation~\eqref{eq:rho} gives
$\rho_r\leq\rho_2=3/8$.
An algorithm that succeeds with probability at least $2/3$
on every labelling also has average success probability at
least $2/3$ under $\mathcal D_r$.
Suppose first that $3q+r+1\leq n$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:quantitative},
\[
    \frac{\binom{3q+r+1}{2}}{n}
    \geq \frac23-\frac38
    =\frac7{24}.
\]
Using $\binom M2\leq M^2/2$, we obtain
    $q
    =\Omega(\sqrt n)$.

In the remaining case, $3q+r+1>n$, so
    $q=\Omega(n)$,
which is stronger. Thus, the algorithm requires
$\Omega(\sqrt n)$ group additions in the worst case.
head: environment

label: lem:reconstruct
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:reconstruct}
Let $|P|=p^a$, and suppose the type of $pP$ is
$(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_s)$, with each $\mu_i\geq1$. Then
\[
 P\cong\left(\bigoplus_{i=1}^s\mathbb Z_{p^{\mu_i+1}}\right)
       \oplus\mathbb Z_p^{\,c},
\]
where the number of additional order-$p$ factors is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reconstruct}
 c=a-\sum_{i=1}^s(\mu_i+1).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $s=\mathop{\rm rank}(pP)\leq\lfloor a/2\rfloor$.
head: environment
name: Reconstruction and rank

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:structure}, $P$ is a direct sum of cyclic groups of
orders $p^\lambda$. Multiplication by $p$ acts separately on each factor.
If $\lambda\geq2$, its image is cyclic of order $p^{\lambda-1}$; if
$\lambda=1$, its image is trivial. Thus every nontrivial factor of $pP$
corresponds to exactly one factor of $P$ with exponent $\mu_i+1$.
All remaining factors of $P$ have order $p$.

Orders multiply in a direct sum, so the sum of the exponents of all factors
of $P$ equals $a$. Subtracting the known exponents proves
\eqref{eq:reconstruct}. Finally each of the $s$ surviving factors uses at
least two powers of $p$ in $|P|$. Therefore $2s\leq a$.
head: environment

label: prop:sutherland
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:sutherland}
Given a prime $p$ and a finite list~$S$ generating an Abelian $p$-group $K$
of rank $s$, a basis and its element orders can be computed deterministically
in
\[
 p^{s/2}\operatorname{poly}(|S|,\log n)
\]
time, if $|K|\leq n$ and group operations take unit time. Neither $|K|$ nor $s$
needs to be given as input.
head: environment
name: Consequence of Sutherland's algorithms

title: Proof
body_md:
We use Algorithms 1 and 4 and Propositions 1--2 of that paper, including
the discrete-logarithm consequence in its Corollary 1. For nontrivial $K$,
we have $s\geq1$. Write $|K|=p^b$ and let its exponent be $p^h$.
The discrete-logarithm cost is (see Section~\ref{TDLC} in the Appendix)
\[
 T_{\rm DL}(K)=O\!\left(
 \frac{\log(h+1)}{\log\log(h+2)}\log|K|
 +\frac bs p^{s/2}\right).
\]
The cost of constructing a basis of $K$ from the generating
set $S$, also summarized in equation~(3) of that paper,
satisfies
\[
 T_{\rm B}(S)=O\!\left(
 \log^{2+\epsilon}|K|+(|S|-s+1)T_{\rm DL}(K)\right)
\]
for fixed $\epsilon>0$, counting group operations.

Set
 $\epsilon=1$. Since $1\leq b,h,s\leq L$, the first bound
gives $T_{\rm DL}(K)=O(\log^2n+ p^{s/2}\log n)$. Substitution into the second gives
 $T_{\rm B}(S)
 =O\!\left(\log^3n+(|S|+1)(\log^2n+p^{s/2}\log n)\right)$.
This is bounded by $p^{s/2}\operatorname{poly}(|S|,\log n)$, as
claimed. Element
orders can be found by repeatedly multiplying by $p$ until the identity
is reached.
head: environment
name: Proof. Derivation from Sutherland

label: lem:generation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:generation}
If $K$ is a finite Abelian $p$-group of rank $s$ and $k\geq s$, then $k$
iid uniform samples fail to generate $K$ with probability at most
$p^{s-k}$.
head: environment
name: Random generation

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ be elements of $K$. Each $a_i$ determines
a coset $a_i+pK$ in the quotient group $K/pK$.
We show that if these cosets span the vector space $K/pK$
over $\mathbb F_p$, then $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ generate~$K$.
Let $U$ be the subgroup generated by the list. Spanning the quotient means
$U+pK=K$, so $K/U=p(K/U)$. Iterating gives $K/U=p^h(K/U)$ for every
positive integer $h$. Choose $p^h$ annihilating $K$. Then $K/U=0$, which
means $U=K$. The converse is immediate by taking images in the quotient.

Recall from Section~\ref{S22} that $K/pK\cong\mathbb F_p^s$.
Take $k$ independent uniform samples from $K$ and consider
their cosets in $K/pK$. Since every coset has the same number
of elements, these cosets correspond to independent uniform
vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_k$ in $\mathbb F_p^s$.
Suppose these vectors do not span $\mathbb F_p^s$. We show that there
is a nonzero linear map $f:\mathbb F_p^s\to\mathbb F_p$ such that
$f(y_i)=0$ for every $i$. Choose a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_t$
of their span, where $t<s$, and extend it to a basis
$v_1,\ldots,v_s$ of $\mathbb F_p^s$. Define
$f(a_1v_1+\cdots+a_sv_s)=a_{t+1}$.
Every sampled vector is a linear combination of
$v_1,\ldots,v_t$, so $f$ is zero on every sampled vector.
However, $f(v_{t+1})=1$, so $f$ is not the zero map.
                                                                  

There are $p^s-1$ nonzero linear maps from $\mathbb F_p^s$ to $\mathbb F_p$:
a linear map is determined by its values on the $s$ basis
vectors, and each value has $p$ choices. For any fixed nonzero
map $f$, exactly $p^{s-1}$ of the $p^s$ vectors satisfy $f(y)=0$.
Thus, a uniform vector satisfies this equality with probability
$1/p$. By independence, all $k$ sampled vectors satisfy it with
probability $p^{-k}$. Since failure to span requires at least
one nonzero map to be zero on all samples, the union bound gives
\[
\mathop{\rm Pr}[y_1,\ldots,y_k\text{ do not span }\mathbb F_p^s]
\leq (p^s-1)p^{-k}
\leq p^{s-k}.
\]
If $s=0$, the quotient is the zero vector space, which is
spanned by every list, so the failure probability is zero.
head: environment

label: lem:sample
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sample}
Write $n=\prod_{p\mid n}p^{a_p}$. For uniform $x\in G$, the element
 $y=({n}/{p^{a_p-1}})x$
is uniform in $pG_p$ and can be computed with $O(\log n)$ table queries.
head: environment
name: Sampling a primary image

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $m_p=n/p^{a_p}$, so that the displayed scalar is $pm_p$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:structure}, multiplication by $m_p$ kills every primary
component other than $G_p$: the order of each such component divides $m_p$.
On $G_p$, multiplication by $m_p$ is invertible because
$\gcd(m_p,p^{a_p})=1$. Explicitly, an integer $u$ with
$um_p\equiv1\pmod{p^{a_p}}$ gives its inverse. Following this map by
multiplication by $p$ therefore maps $G$ onto $pG_p$.

For any homomorphism, the preimages of a point in its image form a coset
of its kernel. All these preimage sets have equal size, so the image of a
uniform element is uniform. Finally, the scalar $pm_p$ is at most $n$.
Repeated doubling and addition, using its binary expansion, computes its
multiple of $x$ in $O(\log n)$ table queries.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show that all sampled subgroups equal their intended images with
high probability. We then bound the cost on every run, including runs on
which some image is not generated.

\paragraph{Correctness.}
Put $s_p=\mathop{\rm rank}(pG_p)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:reconstruct},
$s_p\leq\lfloor a_p/2\rfloor$. Lemmas~\ref{lem:sample}
and~\ref{lem:generation} give
\[
 \mathop{\rm Pr}[K_p\neq pG_p]\leq p^{s_p-k_p}
 \leq2^{-\lceil\log_2 t\rceil+3}\leq\frac1{8t}.
\]
A union bound over the $t$ primes shows that all images are generated with
probability at least $5/6$. On this event, the basis orders returned by
Proposition~\ref{prop:sutherland} describe each whole image. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:reconstruct}, and specifically~\eqref{eq:reconstruct}, the
reconstructed primary types are correct. By Theorem~\ref{thm:structure},
their collection is the type of $G$.

For two groups of equal order, run this procedure on each and compare the
lists. The chance that either type is incorrect is at most $1/3$, again
by a union bound. When both are correct, their comparison decides
isomorphism by Theorem~\ref{thm:structure}.

\paragraph{Cost of the group computations.}
Since $\sum_{p\mid n}a_p\leq\log n$ and $t\leq\log n$, the total
number of samples is
$O(\log n+t\log(t+1))$, which is polynomial in $\log n$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:sample} bounds the cost of forming each image sample.
Even on an unsuccessful run, $K_p$ is a subgroup of $pG_p$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:subgroup-rank} therefore gives
$\mathop{\rm rank}(K_p)\leq s_p$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:sutherland}, the total
basis-subroutine cost is at most
\[
 \widetilde O\!\left(\sum_{p\mid n}p^{s_p/2}\right)
 \leq\widetilde O\!\left(\sum_{p\mid n}p^{a_p/4}\right).
\]
Every summand is at most $n^{1/4}$, and there are at most $\log_2n$ of
them. Thus this cost is $\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$. When $s_p=0$, its summand
is one. Reconstruction and sorting of the integer lists take polynomial
logarithmic time.

\paragraph{Factoring and elementary oracle operations.} We can factor $n$ using the randomized algorithm of Lenstra and
Pomerance~\cite{LenstraPomerance92} that runs in time $n^{o(1)}$ or by
Costa and Harvey~\cite{CostaHarvey12} deterministic
algorithm that runs in time $\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$,
which is sufficient here for factoring the known order $n$. If the identity is not supplied, compute $nx$ for
any input label $x$, using the fact that every element order divides $n$.
If an imported routine needs an inverse, compute $-x=(n-1)x$ by repeated
doubling. These simulations add only logarithmic factors to the cost.
Together, the three cost estimates prove Theorem~\ref{thm:iso}.
head: environment

label: prop:iso-lower
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:iso-lower}
For $n=4^m$, let the hidden group be chosen with equal prior probability
from
\[
 H_0=(\mathbb Z_4)^m
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 H_1=(\mathbb Z_4)^{m-1}\oplus(\mathbb Z_2)^2.
\]
Conditional on this choice, give the algorithm a uniform random relabeling
with a fixed identity label. Distinguishing the two cases with average
success probability at least $2/3$ requires $\Omega(n^{1/4})$ queries.
head: environment
name: Bshouty's decision lower bound

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the same symbolic simulation for both groups and compare
each actual execution with this simulation. The simulation does
not depend on which group was chosen. Thus, any advantage in
distinguishing the groups must come from an unexpected equality
between the evaluations of distinct formal expressions.

\paragraph{A common symbolic simulation.}
First fix the algorithm's random coins. Use the symbolic
simulation from Section~\ref{sec:coupling}, with coefficients
in $\mathbb Z_4$. The two groups have the same order, and multiplying
any element of either group by four gives zero. The simulation
therefore has the same distribution in both cases: its answers
depend only on formal sums and random choices of labels,
without using the values assigned to the formal symbols.

A decision algorithm outputs a bit rather than a group label.
Thus, by~\eqref{eq:count}, an algorithm performing at most $q$
group additions registers at most $M=3q+1$ distinct formal
expressions, including the expression $0$ for the identity.
Assume first that $M\leq n$.

\paragraph{Collision probabilities.}
Fix the complete symbolic transcript. The formal expressions
are now fixed, while the elements assigned to the formal
symbols remain independent and uniform in the chosen group.

Consider the difference of two distinct formal expressions.
If some coefficient is odd, multiplication by that coefficient
is a bijection on $H_j$. The corresponding multiple of an
independent uniform element is therefore uniform in $H_j$.
Adding the other terms preserves uniformity, so the two
expressions have the same evaluation with probability $1/n$.

Otherwise, all coefficients are even, and at least one
coefficient is two. Doubling a uniform element of $H_j$ gives
a uniform element of $2H_j$, because every element of $2H_j$
has the same number of preimages under doubling. The other
terms also belong to $2H_j$. Their sum with the independent
uniform term is therefore uniform in $2H_j$, so the collision
probability is $1/|2H_j|$. Here,
 $|2H_0|=2^m$,
 and $|2H_1|=2^{m-1}$.
In either coefficient case, a pair collides with probability
at most $2^{-m}$ in $H_0$ and at most $2^{-(m-1)}$ in $H_1$.

There are at most $\binom M2$ pairs of distinct registered
expressions. Applying the union bound and then averaging over
the symbolic transcript, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:collision},
bounds the probability of $\mathsf{Bad}$ in each group by
\[
 \epsilon_0:=\binom M2\,2^{-m},
 \qquad
 \epsilon_1:=\binom M2\,2^{-(m-1)}.
\]

\paragraph{Success when the two groups are equally likely.}
Choose $j\in\{0,1\}$ uniformly. Since the symbolic simulation
is independent of $j$, the bit it outputs equals $j$ with
probability exactly $1/2$.

For each fixed $j$, Lemma~\ref{lem:coupling} compares the actual
execution on a uniformly random labeling of $H_j$ with the
symbolic simulation. Outside $\mathsf{Bad}$, their outputs agree.
Therefore, if the actual execution outputs $j$, either the
simulation also outputs $j$ or $\mathsf{Bad}$ occurs. The actual
success probability can consequently exceed the simulated
success probability by at most $\epsilon_j$.

Averaging over the two choices of $j$ gives
\[
 \mathop{\rm Pr}[\text{correct decision}]
 \leq \frac12+\frac{\epsilon_0+\epsilon_1}{2}
 = \frac12+\frac32
   \frac{\binom{3q+1}{2}}{\sqrt n},
\]
where we used $n=4^m$. This bound holds for every fixed choice
of the algorithm's random coins. Averaging over those coins
therefore gives the same bound for randomized algorithms.

An algorithm that succeeds with probability at least $2/3$
on every input also succeeds with probability at least $2/3$
under this random choice of group and labeling. Hence,
\[
 \binom{3q+1}{2}\geq \frac{\sqrt n}{9},
\]
which implies $q=\Omega(n^{1/4})$.

Finally, if $M>n$, then
 $q>{(n-1)}/{3}=\Omega(n)$,
which is stronger than the required lower bound.
head: environment

label: cor:iso-tight
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:iso-tight}
Two finite Abelian groups of known order $n$ can be tested
for isomorphism with probability at least $2/3$ in
$\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$ time. Every randomized algorithm
with this success guarantee requires $\Omega(n^{1/4})$
group additions in the worst case along the orders $n=4^m$.
Thus, the time bound is optimal up to factors polynomial
in $\log n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The upper bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:iso}. For the lower bound, compare the
unknown group in Proposition~\ref{prop:iso-lower} with a canonical copy of
$H_0$, represented by coordinates modulo four. Its table answers can be
computed without querying the unknown input. An isomorphism tester would
therefore solve the distinction in Proposition~\ref{prop:iso-lower} with
no greater number of unknown-table queries.
head: environment

label: cor:explicit-iso
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:explicit-iso}
Suppose a randomized algorithm, given a group
$G\cong\mathbb F_2^r$, outputs a description of an isomorphism
$f:\mathbb F_2^r\longrightarrow G$ with probability at least $2/3$
on every relabeling. Count all group additions used to
construct this description and to obtain the actual labels
of $f(e_1),\ldots,f(e_r)$. Their total worst-case number is
$\Omega(\sqrt n)$, where $n=2^r$.

If these labels can be obtained from the description without
further group additions, then constructing the description
alone requires $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ group additions in the
worst case.

name: Constructing and evaluating an isomorphism

title: Proof
body_md:
Run the algorithm and evaluate its output on
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$. Whenever the algorithm produces a correct
isomorphism, the resulting labels
$f(e_1),\ldots,f(e_r)$ form a basis of $G$. This procedure
therefore constructs a basis with probability at least
$2/3$ on every relabeling. Theorem~\ref{thm:main} implies
that it requires $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ group additions in the
worst case.
